533.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: an inheritance (Deuteronomy 33:4)
533.hook: the Torah is "the inheritance of the congregation of Jacob", learned from childhood
533.howItsDone: Following the Talmud, the verse 'Torah tzivah lanu Moshe' is traditionally among the first a young child learns, often sung, together with the first line of the Shema.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses' last words: blessings, tribe by tribe. Your line was end with a blessing. Today, one verse from among those blessings, the one the Talmud says a child learns first.

What's the first sentence you remember learning by heart? A nursery rhyme, a prayer at bedtime, a pledge at school, a line from a song. Whatever it was, it may still be in there, word for word. The Talmud says that when a Jewish child first begins to talk, there's a particular verse a parent should teach. It isn't from Genesis, at the beginning of everything. It's from the very end of the Torah, tucked in among Moses' blessings.
screen: `A RHYME, A PLEDGE, A SONG.` → `STILL THERE, WORD FOR WORD.` → `A CHILD'S FIRST VERSE.`

segments.voice: "Moses commanded us a law, An inheritance of the congregation of Jacob." In Hebrew: Torah tzivah lanu Moshe, morashah kehillat Ya'akov. The Talmud, in Sukkah, says that as soon as a child can speak, the father teaches him this verse, along with the first line of the Shema. Notice the little word lanu, to us. A child's first verse already says we. Now the second half. Morashah, inheritance. And whose inheritance is it? Not the priests'. Not the scholars'. The congregation of Jacob: everyone. Maimonides makes the point sharply. Israel was given three crowns, he writes. The crown of priesthood went to Aaron's family. The crown of kingship went to David's line. But the crown of Torah is set out for anyone who wants it: whoever wishes may come and take it. The Talmud also plays with the word. It reads morashah, inheritance, as if it said me'orasah, betrothed: the Torah isn't only handed down like property; it's meant to be loved. And some teachers notice that Hebrew has two words for inheritance. Yerushah is what you receive. Morashah, they suggest, is a heritage you hold in order to pass it on. Either way, the first verse a child learns says: this belongs to you, and to all of us.

534.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: from the mountain (Deuteronomy 34:1–4)
534.hook: from Mount Nebo Moses sees the land he won't enter
534.tomorrow: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)
534.howItsDone: The final chapter of Deuteronomy, with Moses on Mount Nebo, is read on Simchat Torah; in many communities its closing verses are read with special honor as the end of the yearly Torah cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, morashah, the inheritance of everyone. Your line was inheritance for everyone. Today, Moses climbs one last mountain.

Grandparents plant trees their grandchildren will sit under. Founders start things they'll have to hand on. A child fully grown, a cause won, a garden that will only be beautiful in thirty years: most people carry at least one goal they may not live to see finished. It's one of the strangest human habits, working hard toward a place you may never stand in. Moses spent forty years walking toward a land. Today he gets to see it.
screen: `A TREE FOR THE GRANDCHILDREN.` → `A PLACE YOU MAY NEVER STAND.` → `FORTY YEARS, AND A VIEW.`

segments.voice: Moses goes up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, across from Jericho. And God shows him the land: Gilead as far as Dan, the lands of the tribes, the hill country, the plain, all the way to the western sea, and the Negev in the south. Then God says: "This is the land which I swore unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob, saying: I will give it unto thy seed; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither." He sees all of it. He will not enter. Earlier, in Va'etchanan, Moses had pleaded to be allowed across. A midrash counts his pleading as five hundred fifteen prayers, the number value of the Hebrew word va'etchanan, and I pleaded. The answer was still no. And yet here he climbs anyway. The text records no complaint at the top. Only seeing. Some commentators read the view as a gift. Rashi says God showed Moses not just the land but its future, what would happen there to his people for generations. Others read it simply. He saw the place he'd led everyone toward, and the text lets that be enough. A mountain traditionally identified as Nebo still stands in Jordan today, looking west. The Torah doesn't hide the cost. He doesn't arrive. But he's allowed to see.

535.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: no one knows his grave (Deuteronomy 34:5–6)
535.hook: God buries Moses, and no one knows his grave to this day
535.howItsDone: Jewish tradition calls caring for the dead chesed shel emet, a true kindness, since it can't be repaid; local chevra kadisha societies prepare bodies for burial, and tradition places Moses' death on the 7th of Adar, a day some burial societies mark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the view from Nebo. Your line was see it from the mountain. Today, the death of Moses, and a strange detail about his grave.

Pyramids. Mausoleums. A marble tomb with a line of visitors outside. Famous people are often given famous graves, and pilgrims travel far to stand where a founder lies, leaving flowers, candles, notes, stones. Some tombs become places of prayer. Moses, the teacher at the center of the Torah, dies on a mountain in Moab. And the text goes out of its way to tell us there is nothing to visit.
screen: `PYRAMIDS AND MAUSOLEUMS.` → `PILGRIMS AT THE TOMB.` → `NOTHING TO VISIT.`

segments.voice: So Moses, the servant of God, dies there in the land of Moab, at God's word. He is buried in a valley opposite Beth-peor, the text says, "and no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day." Who buried him? The Hebrew simply says: he buried him. Rashi says it was God, in His glory. The Talmud, in Sotah, takes that seriously and turns it into a teaching about how people should live. God clothed Adam and Eve. God visited Abraham when he was healing. God comforted Isaac when he mourned. And God buried Moses. So, the Talmud says, walk in God's ways: clothe, visit, comfort, bury. When volunteers of a chevra kadisha, a Jewish burial society, care for the body of someone who has died, they're walking in that line. And the hidden grave? The text doesn't say why. One explanation often given is that the people would have made it a place of worship, and Moses had always pointed beyond himself. Whatever the reason, the effect is clear. No shrine. No relic. What remains of Moses is what he taught. And the teaching isn't left in one place. It's in each Torah scroll, read aloud week by week. Moses' grave is unknown. His words are read wherever the scroll is opened.

V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. A portion that ends with a death, an unknown grave, and a teaching that stays.

536.title: V'Zot HaBerachah: face to face (Deuteronomy 34:10–12)
536.hook: no prophet arose like Moses, "whom the LORD knew face to face"
536.howItsDone: In Jewish speech Moses is commonly called Moshe Rabbenu, 'Moses our teacher', and the closing verses of Deuteronomy are read on Simchat Torah as the yearly Torah cycle ends.

segments.voice: Yesterday in V'Zot HaBerachah, the grave no one knows. Your line was no grave, only teaching. Today, the Torah's last word about Moses himself.

A teacher stays after class to explain it one more time. A coach sees something in a kid before the kid does. A grandparent explains the world over breakfast. People like this rarely ask for credit, and often never hear what they did. Their names fade, while what they taught keeps going. The Torah's final verses are, in a way, a tribute to a teacher. They say who Moses was, now that he's gone.
screen: `A TEACHER AFTER CLASS.` → `A GRANDPARENT AT BREAKFAST.` → `A TRIBUTE AT THE END.`

segments.voice: "And there hath not arisen a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face." Then the verses recall the signs in Egypt and the mighty hand, done in the sight of all Israel. Face to face: in Hebrew, panim el panim. Earlier, in Numbers, God explains the difference to Moses' own brother and sister: with other prophets I speak in visions and dreams, but with Moses, mouth to mouth. The text presents that closeness as direct, unlike any other. Maimonides made that uniqueness one of his thirteen principles of faith: that Moses' prophecy stands above that of every other prophet. And yet, notice the title Jewish tradition actually gives him. Not Moses our prophet. Not Moses our king. Moshe Rabbenu: Moses our teacher. He led slaves out of Egypt, stood at the sea, met God on a mountain, and the name that stuck is teacher. There's a quiet second meaning in face to face. It describes something no one else had: God and Moses. But a teacher is known face to face too, by the students sitting across the table. In the tradition, Moses' closeness to God reaches later generations through what he taught. The book closes, and the tribute it chooses is this: he was known, close up. And through him, so were the words.

V'Zot HaBerachah. And this is the blessing. Ending with Moses, known face to face, and remembered as our teacher.

537.title: Simchat Torah close: the circle
537.hook: the Torah's last letter and first letter spell lev, heart; the scroll rolls straight on
537.howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, congregations dance with the Torah scrolls in seven circuits (hakafot), read the end of Deuteronomy, and immediately begin Genesis again; the two readers are honored as chatan Torah and chatan Bereshit, and some communities honor women with parallel titles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses, known face to face, and remembered as our teacher. Your line was face to face. Today, the Torah's very last word, and what happens right after it.

On Simchat Torah, synagogues get loud. The scrolls come out of the ark and people dance with them, around and around the room, seven circuits, sometimes spilling out into the street. Children wave flags. Someone who hasn't set foot inside all year is handed a scroll to hold. And in the middle of all that, something quiet and precise happens at the reading table. The last words of the Torah are read aloud. And then, without stopping, the first.
screen: `SCROLLS OUT OF THE ARK.` → `SEVEN CIRCUITS OF DANCING.` → `THE LAST WORDS, THEN THE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Deuteronomy ends with the words in the sight of all Israel; in Hebrew, le'einei kol Yisrael. So the last letter of the whole Torah is the lamed at the end of Yisrael. Genesis begins with bereshit, in the beginning, and its first letter is bet. Put the last letter and the first together, lamed and bet, and they spell lev: heart. Some teachers point this out. The Torah, end joined to beginning, makes a heart. On Simchat Torah, the person honored with reading the end is called the chatan Torah, the bridegroom of the Torah. The one honored with starting again is the chatan Bereshit, the bridegroom of the beginning. The scroll isn't rolled up and put away for a rest. It's rolled straight back to its start, and the same day the reading begins again: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Since day three hundred thirty-two, this path has walked from the plagues in Egypt through the rest of Exodus, through Leviticus and Numbers, and these last weeks through Deuteronomy, Moses' farewell. The forgotten sheaf and the first fruits. Choose life. Write your own. The song, the blessing, the grave no one knows, face to face. Tomorrow a new part of the year begins: the siddur, the prayer book, walked page by page. But the Torah doesn't stop. The end touches the beginning.
screen: `LE'EINEI KOL YISRAEL.` · `LAMED AND BET SPELL LEV.` · `TWO BRIDEGROOMS OF THE TORAH.` · `ROLLED STRAIGHT BACK TO THE START.` · then, large: `THE END TOUCHES THE BEGINNING.`

Notice what it's like to finish and start in the same breath, and where something ending in your own life might touch a beginning.
Lev. Heart — the word spelled when the Torah's last letter and its first letter are joined, on the day the ending touches the beginning.
Your line: the end touches the beginning. The scroll is rolled straight back to its start. Day five hundred thirty-seven.

538.title: The siddur
538.hook: the prayer book, named "order", the most-used Jewish book after the Torah
538.howItsDone: Jews who pray daily use a siddur for the morning, afternoon and evening services, and a related book, the machzor, for the High Holy Days. Different communities follow different rites (nusach), such as Ashkenaz, Sefard and Edot HaMizrach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the circle: the Torah's last letter and its first, together spelling lev, heart. Your line was the end touches the beginning. Today, a new book.

Near the door of a synagogue there's often a shelf of matching books, worn soft at the corners. One page carries a wine stain from a holiday, another a child's pencil mark, another the crease of a hand that held it for a lifetime. People take one on the way in without thinking. It isn't the Torah scroll. But for a Jew who prays every day, it may be the book held more often than any other. For the next stretch of this year, this path walks through it, in order.
screen: `A SHELF BY THE DOOR.` → `WORN SOFT AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE BOOK HELD MOST OFTEN.`

segments.voice: The word is siddur. It comes from seder, order, the same root as the Passover seder, the ordered meal. A siddur is the prayer book: the weekday prayers, the Sabbath and festival prayers, blessings for food and for waking up, all arranged in the order they're said. That order is the point. Jewish prayer isn't mostly a blank page. It has a shape: blessings, then psalms, then the Shema, then the standing prayer, then the closing. The Talmud discusses many of these prayers long before anyone bound them into one volume. Among the oldest written orders of prayer that survive are two from the geonim, the heads of the academies in Babylonia: the order of Rav Amram Gaon, and the siddur of Rav Saadia Gaon. Since then, many versions have grown. Ashkenazi Jews, from Central and Eastern Europe, have their rite. Sephardi and Mizrahi Jews, from Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, have theirs. Yemenite communities, Hasidic communities and the modern movements each have siddurim of their own. The core is shared; the details differ, and each community keeps its own. Why give prayer an order at all? One answer: on the days you have no words, the siddur has them. On the days you have too many, it gives them a path. Starting tomorrow, it opens, step by step.

segments.voice: If you have a siddur, take it off the shelf, feel its weight, and open it anywhere to read one line, in Hebrew or in translation. If you don't, hold any book you've gone back to many times, and remember that people have prayed these words, in this order, from books like this, across many generations.
Siddur. Order. The Jewish prayer book: the daily prayers, arranged in the order they're said.
Your line: prayer has an order. On the days you have no words, it has them. See you tomorrow.

539.title: Three times a day (Berakhot 26b)
539.hook: morning, afternoon and evening prayer are linked to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, or to the Temple offerings
539.howItsDone: Observant Jews pray three services daily: shacharit in the morning, minchah in the afternoon and ma'ariv (also called arvit) in the evening, often with a minyan, a quorum of ten, in synagogue.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the siddur, the book of order. Your line was prayer has an order. Today, the first order inside it: when.

Breakfast, lunch, dinner. Waking up, the afternoon slump, winding down at night. Most people already live by a rhythm of three, and three times a day the mood tips into something new. Jewish prayer hangs on the same three hinges: shacharit in the morning, minchah in the afternoon, ma'ariv in the evening. The Talmud asks where these three times came from. It gives two answers, and keeps both.
screen: `BREAKFAST, LUNCH, DINNER.` → `SHACHARIT, MINCHAH, MA'ARIV.` → `TWO ANSWERS, BOTH KEPT.`

segments.voice: In Berakhot, on page twenty-six, Rabbi Yose son of Rabbi Hanina says the patriarchs set the prayers. Abraham set the morning: the Torah says he rose early and went to the place where he had stood before God. Isaac set the afternoon: "And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." Jacob set the evening: night was falling when he came upon a certain place, and the Talmud reads that word, vayifga, as meeting God in prayer. Rabbi Yehoshua son of Levi says something else: the prayers match the Temple's daily offerings, morning and afternoon, with the evening prayer matching the parts that burned on the altar through the night. The Talmud doesn't throw either answer away. It weaves them together: the patriarchs began these prayers, and the rabbis tied them to the offerings. One picture says prayer is personal, a man walking alone in a field at dusk. The other says it's shared and regular, like the Temple's daily service. Both stay on the same page. And so a week that began in the Torah's last chapters, with Moses seeing the land from the mountain and buried where no one knows, ends inside the prayer book: its order, and now its three times a day.
screen: `ABRAHAM: THE MORNING.` · `ISAAC: IN THE FIELD AT EVENTIDE.` · `JACOB: MEETING THE PLACE AT NIGHT.` · `OR: THE TEMPLE'S DAILY OFFERINGS.` · then, large: `MORNING, AFTERNOON, EVENING.`

segments.voice: Pick three moments, one for morning, one for afternoon, one for night, and tie each to something you already do: the first coffee, a late-afternoon break, brushing your teeth. Picture stopping at each for three breaths, like hinges in your day. If you pray, it could be a prayer you know; if not, the pause alone is enough.
Vayifga. He met, or encountered — the word the Talmud reads in Jacob's story as meeting God in prayer, one root of the three daily prayer times.
Your line: morning, afternoon, evening. Three hinges, and two old answers for why. Day five hundred thirty-nine, done.
